questions.question: What is the prototype chain? How does JavaScript implement inheritance?
questions.answer:
Every JavaScript object has an internal [[Prototype]] slot pointing to another object (or null). When you access a property, JS first checks the object itself, then walks up the prototype chain until it finds it or reaches null.

This is prototypal inheritance — objects inherit from other objects, not from classes. The class keyword (ES6) is syntactic sugar over this prototype-based system.
questions.tip: Object.create is the purest way to show prototypal inheritance without class syntax — use it in interviews to show depth.
followUps: What is the difference between __proto__ and prototype?
How does Object.create differ from new?

questions.question: What is the difference between __proto__, prototype, and Object.getPrototypeOf()?
questions.answer:
prototype: A property on constructor functions/classes. When you call new Foo(), the created object's [[Prototype]] is set to Foo.prototype. Only functions have a meaningful .prototype.

__proto__: A non-standard (now legacy) getter/setter on object instances that exposes [[Prototype]]. Deprecated in favour of Object.getPrototypeOf().

Object.getPrototypeOf(obj): The official ES5+ way to read [[Prototype]] of any object. Use this in production code.
questions.tip: Never use __proto__ in production — it's a legacy accessor. Always use Object.getPrototypeOf() and Object.setPrototypeOf().
followUps: Why is mutating prototype at runtime bad for performance?

questions.question: How does class syntax compile down to prototype-based code? What does Babel do with a class?
questions.answer:
A class is a constructor function with methods placed on its .prototype. Babel compiles:

- The constructor becomes a regular function.
- Class methods are added to Constructor.prototype via Object.defineProperty (non-enumerable).
- extends sets up the prototype chain: Child.prototype = Object.create(Parent.prototype) and Child.__proto__ = Parent (for static inheritance).
- super() in the constructor calls the parent constructor with the right context.
questions.tip: Understanding what Babel produces is asked directly at Meta and Google. It shows you know JS, not just the syntax.
followUps: Why are class methods non-enumerable but prototype methods added manually ARE enumerable?
What is the difference between super() and super.method()?

questions.title: prototype method lookup
questions.explanation:
Output: "Cat speaks" then false
a.speak() is found on Animal.prototype via the prototype chain — not directly on a. hasOwnProperty('speak') = false because speak lives on the prototype, not the instance. Only name is an own property of a.
questions.concept: Prototype chain lookup — own vs inherited

questions.title: Constructor vs prototype property
questions.explanation:
Output: "Hi Alice"
When a property exists on BOTH the instance and the prototype, the instance's own property wins — prototype is only checked if the property isn't found directly on the object. p.greet is set in the constructor body (own property), so it shadows the prototype method.

questions.title: Shared prototype mutation
questions.explanation:
Output: ['engine']
parts is on the prototype — shared by ALL instances. c1.parts.push('engine') mutates the array on the prototype. c2.parts refers to the same array. This is a classic prototype mutation pitfall. Fix: initialise parts in the constructor (this.parts = []) to give each instance its own array.

questions.title: Prototype chain — instanceof
questions.explanation:
Output: true true true
b's prototype chain: b → B.prototype → A.prototype → Object.prototype → null. instanceof checks if the constructor's prototype exists anywhere in the chain. B.prototype: yes. A.prototype: yes (set via Object.create). Object.prototype: yes (always). All three are true.

questions.title: class vs prototype — are they the same?
questions.explanation:
Output: "function" false "function"
class is syntactic sugar over functions. typeof Animal = "function". speak is defined on Animal.prototype (not on the instance), so hasOwnProperty('speak') = false. typeof Animal.prototype.speak = "function". Classes do NOT create a new type — they are constructor functions under the hood.
questions.concept: class is syntactic sugar over prototype

questions.title: this in prototype method — gotcha
questions.explanation:
Output: 0
When inc is extracted from c and called as inc(), this is no longer c — in strict mode it's undefined (TypeError), in sloppy mode it's the global object. this.count++ increments the global count (or throws), not c.count. c.count stays 0. Always call methods as obj.method() to preserve this context.

questions.title: Object.create vs new — proto chain
questions.explanation:
Output: "Hello from World" then false
Object.create(base) creates obj with base as its prototype. greet is on the prototype (base), not on obj itself. hasOwnProperty('greet') = false. But obj.greet() works because the prototype chain finds greet on base, and this = obj so this.name = 'World'.
